{{short description|Number whose divisors summed twice over equal twice itself}}

In [[number theory]], a '''superperfect number''' is a positive [[integer]] {{mvar|n}} that satisfies

:<math>\sigma^2(n)=\sigma(\sigma(n))=2n\, ,</math>

where {{mvar|σ}} is the [[divisor function|sum-of-divisors function]]. Superperfect numbers are not a generalization of [[perfect number]]s but have a common generalization. The term was coined by D. Suryanarayana (1969).<ref name=Guy99 />

The first few superperfect numbers are:

:[[2 (number)|2]], [[4 (number)|4]], [[16 (number)|16]], [[64 (number)|64]], [[4096 (number)|4096]], [[65536 (number)|65536]], 262144, 1073741824, ... {{OEIS|id=A019279}}.

To illustrate: it can be seen that 16 is a superperfect number as {{nowrap|1=σ(16) = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31}}, and {{nowrap|1=σ(31) = 1 + 31 = 32}}, thus {{nowrap|1=σ(σ(16)) = 32 = 2 × 16}}.

If {{mvar|n}} is an ''[[Parity (mathematics)|even]]'' superperfect number, then {{mvar|n}} must be a [[power of 2]], {{math|2<sup>''k''</sup>}}, such that {{math|2<sup>''k''+1</sup> − 1}} is a [[Mersenne prime]].<ref name="Guy99" /><ref name="mathworld">{{MathWorld|urlname=SuperperfectNumber |title=Superperfect Number }}</ref>

It is not known whether there are any [[Odd number|odd]] superperfect numbers. An odd superperfect number {{mvar|n}} would have to be a [[square number]] such that either {{mvar|n}} or {{math|''σ''(''n'')}} is divisible by at least three distinct primes.<ref name=mathworld /> There are no odd superperfect numbers below 7{{e|24}}.<ref name=Guy99>Guy (2004) p. 99.</ref>

== Generalizations ==
Perfect and superperfect numbers are examples of the wider class of ''m''-superperfect numbers, which satisfy

:<math> \sigma^m(n) = 2n , </math>

corresponding to ''m'' = 1 and 2 respectively.  For ''m'' ≥ 3 there are no even ''m''-superperfect numbers.<ref name=Guy99 />

The ''m''-superperfect numbers are in turn examples of (''m'',''k'')-perfect numbers which satisfy<ref>Cohen & te Riele (1996)</ref>

:<math>\sigma^m(n)=kn\, .</math>

With this notation, perfect numbers are (1,2)-perfect, [[multiperfect number]]s are (1,''k'')-perfect,  superperfect numbers are (2,2)-perfect and ''m''-superperfect numbers are (''m'',2)-perfect.<ref>Guy (2007) p.79</ref>  Examples of classes of (''m'',''k'')-perfect numbers are:
